concept:
The site is a worked-out limestone quarry cut west into a hillside. Two made-up levels survive: the PAN, the old working floor, a flat irregular platform roughly 300 by 250 m; and the BENCH, an 11.4 m higher terrace running along the western rim, which carried the plant yard and the weighbridge. Two ramps join them and they are not the same ramp. La Discesa was the loaded haul road: it leaves the bench at its northern nose, breaks over the crest of the face at 3% for thirty metres and then falls at 8% straight down the face to the pan. La Rampa is the empty-return road: shorter in plan, 7.81% the other way, and it switchbacks at the top because a return ramp always does. The circuit is that ground with asphalt on it.

The organising idea is the CIK-FIA 2026 vertical-radius rule read forwards instead of as an obstacle. R = V^2/K means the horizontal length a gradient change occupies scales with the square of the speed at which it is taken. An 8% break at 136 km/h needs 73 m of road; the same 8% break at 56 km/h needs 18 m. So on a kart circuit the elevation cannot be distributed as taste dictates: every crest and every compression is priced in metres of straight, and the only places you can afford a violent one are the slow ones. That single fact laid this circuit out. The two blind moments in the lap - the brow at Il Salto and the crest inside the Ciglione hairpin - are at 114 km/h and 56 km/h because those are the two places where 5.0% and 8.5% of gradient change would fit. The fast half of the lap, T3 through T5 and the whole pan straight, is dead flat at 0.00% longitudinal because nothing else is legal at 125-138 km/h in the space available. That is not a compromise; it is what a kart circuit on a hill looks like.

Two derived results run through the whole design and are worth stating because they are not obvious. First, the regulation's minimum radius is exactly a cap on vertical acceleration, and the cap is speed-independent: a = v^2/R with R = (3.6v)^2/K gives a = K/12.96, which is 1.543 m/s^2 (0.157 g) for a concave profile and 1.157 m/s^2 (0.118 g) for a convex one, at any speed whatsoever. No legal kart circuit can compress a kart harder than +15.7% normal load or lift it lighter than -11.8%. Both compressions on this lap are built at the minimum radius and therefore at exactly 0.157 g, which is +27.5 kgf on a 175 kg kart. Second, the sight time over a minimum-radius crest has a floor of 1.79 s that depends only on K and on how low the driver sits - t = 3.6*V*d/(2K) + 3.6*C/(2*d*V) with C = (sqrt(2*h_eye)+sqrt(2*h_target))^2, minimised at 2*3.6*sqrt(C/(4K)) independent of V. Cava Vecchia's two crests measure 1.86 s and 1.97 s. A crest built to the regulation minimum is inherently about two seconds blind, and that is why both of this circuit's blind moments feel the same however fast you are going through them.

segments.label: Rettilineo del Banco - start/finish, line to T1
Il Salto - approach, still on the bench
Il Salto - la rottura, the lead-in grade over the face crest
Il Salto - the drop, down the face
La Conca - the hollow, run-out onto the pan
Rettilineo del Fondo - the pan straight
Piede della Rampa - the ramp foot, over the sump
Il Banco Sud - last corner to the start line

measured.min_separation_where: the top of La Rampa at 1231.6 m against Il Banco Sud at 1271.8 m - the return ramp passing the start straight on the far side of the Ciglione switchback. With a 9 m and a 10 m road that is 24.4 m of clear ground between asphalt edges against the regulation's 6 m minimum. Both are within 1 m of each other in elevation there, so the separation is a genuine plan clearance and not a bridge.
measured.notes: The walk is the brief's, at 0.25 m, run on segment lengths rounded to 0.01 m from the least-squares closure solve; the 17 mm closure error is that rounding and nothing else. Every straight run merged across collinear segments: 196.92 m (Il Salto, begins 327.5 m), 194.34 m (Piede + Rampa, begins 1043.2 m), 188.26 m (start straight, begins 1265.8 m), 157.48 m (Fondo), 153.87 m (Il Banco), 63.88 m (Piazzale), 37.59 m (Sponda). All inside the 200 m cap; the tightest margin is 3.08 m at Il Salto. Elevation datum is the start line: the highest point on the lap is +0.62 m at the exit of T7a and the lowest is -10.80 m at the foot of La Rampa. Lap time is a forward/backward pass over a 1 m grid using the measured lock sweep for corner caps, 1.53 g braking corrected for grade, and a tractive model calibrated so 0-100 km/h takes the measured 4.50 s. It assumes the kart sits exactly on its limit everywhere and takes no account of tire scrub, shift torque cuts or line compromise, so treat 44.0 s as an optimistic floor and 47-49 s as the number a driver would see.

corners.name: T1
corners.provokes: The regulation first corner, and the one place the elevation rule is visible by its absence. Art 7.6 wants the first corner 'open as much as possible' and 8-12 m wide, and a direction change of at least 45 deg is what makes it the first corner at all; this is exactly 45 deg at the regulation's maximum 12 m. It is on the bench and therefore at a constant -0.70%, because a gradient change 113 m after a standing start would be a change in a start-and-acceleration section, which is the case the 2026 text names first.
corners.cliff_note: Design line radius 60.3 m, which is beyond the 58.49 m row of the sweep and therefore at the 1.86 g plateau. Steering demand is well under a fifth of lock. Nothing about #137 is in play here.
corners.kerb: Red/white 1 m alternation, inside only, 30 mm profile. No exit kerb: the exit is the entry to a 154 m straight and a kerb there would only bounce a kart towards the pit wall.
corners.runoff: 45 deg is under the 80 deg threshold, so no axial run-off is mandatory. The failure mode is running wide, which leaves the road at a shallow angle: 6 m of compacted apron then a continuous smooth vertical barrier along the outside per art 8 for probable impact angles under 30 deg. Sized against the 133 km/h approach as a glancing contact, not a stop.
corners.rollover_note: Right-hander, 2.81 g threshold, sustained 1.86 g. Margin 1.51x.

corners.name: T2
corners.provokes: The corner that exists because the vertical rule says it has to. Il Salto's 5.0% break needs 43.2 m of transition at the speed it is taken; taken at 137 km/h it would need 199 m and there is nowhere to put it. So the road has to be slow at the rim, and this is what makes it slow. It is also the sharpest speed change on the lap - 137 to 67 km/h - and the corner whose exit is punished hardest, because a bad one is paid for down 82 m of 8% descent and then 157 m of pan straight.
corners.cliff_note: Design line radius 26.8 m sits between the sweep's 18.99 m / 0.88 g row and its 32.64 m / 1.59 g row, interpolating to about 1.29 g. That is roughly a quarter of lock - the exact place #137 starts to bite. A driver who arrives 10 km/h hot adds lock and finds the scrub, and the scrub happens on the rim of an 11 m face.
corners.kerb: Red/white inside kerb, 30 mm, and a raised outside kerb on the exit - the only one on the circuit - because the outside of T2 is the crest of the face and the kerb is the first element of the edge protection, not a track-limits device.
corners.runoff: Sized against the 137 km/h approach, not the 67 km/h apex, because this is the heaviest braking zone on the lap. 6 m of compacted apron at no more than 10% away from the track, then a 22 m gravel bed at the art 8.2 minimum 2 m width and 300 mm depth, then a tire barrier. A kart that loses it at the apex stops in 19.7 m of gravel. A kart that arrives with no brakes at all reaches the barrier at 120 km/h, which is why the barrier line is set 8 m inside the crest of the face and the crest itself carries the quarry's own rock berm behind it.
corners.rollover_note: Right-hander, 2.81 g threshold, 1.29 g sustained. Not a rollover corner; it is a scrub corner.

corners.name: T3
corners.provokes: The first thing you meet after the compression, and therefore the corner that tests whether a compression means anything. Turn-in is 39 m past the end of the sag's vertical curve, so the kart has just been loaded to +15.7% normal load and is shedding it as it turns. 97 m of corner at 125 km/h is 2.8 s of steady 1.85 g. It is also the only 90 deg direction change on the lap that is taken fast, which is what makes it the corner that needs the most run-off and the reason it is out on the open pan where there is room for it.
corners.cliff_note: Design line radius 66.3 m, on the 1.86 g plateau, under a fifth of lock. The only way to reach #137's territory here is to have already lost the car.
corners.kerb: Red/white inside kerb over the middle 60 deg of the arc, 30 mm. No outside kerb - the outside is the gravel bed's approach apron and a kerb there would launch a kart into it.
corners.runoff: Sized against 138 km/h. 10 m of compacted apron, 35 m of gravel, then a continuous smooth barrier at a shallow angle rather than a head-on stop, because a kart that loses a 62 m corner leaves it tangentially at well under 30 deg. Straight-on from the 125 km/h apex would need 82 m of gravel to stop, which is why the barrier here is the art 8 small-angle type and the gravel is a decelerator rather than a stopper. This is the widest run-off on the circuit and the reason the fast half of the lap is on the pan.
corners.rollover_note: Right-hander, 2.81 g threshold, 1.85 g sustained. Margin 1.52x. In the reverse layout this same corner is a LEFT at the same speed, margin 1.31x, which is the single biggest difference between the two directions.

corners.name: T4
corners.provokes: The overtaking corner, and the answer to the brief's warning that a kart braking zone is 20-50 m. It is not built out of braking distance - 33 m is all this kart has from 138 km/h - it is built out of ENTRY WIDTH. 14 m, the widest on the circuit, which is 8 m of regulation minimum plus 6 m bought specifically to hold two lines. The exit then does the work: T4 is a right and T5 is a left, so the kart that took the inside at T4 exits on the wrong side of a 64 m apron for a 79 m left-hander that is on the throttle the whole way.
corners.cliff_note: Design line radius 32.3 m, essentially the sweep's 32.64 m / 1.59 g / 81.3 km/h row exactly. The extra 6 m of road width is what keeps it there: at the 8 m regulation minimum the same 26 m centerline radius gives a 29.3 m line and about 1.42 g, and the corner would sit the wrong side of quarter lock. The width is a #137 mitigation as much as a racing one.
corners.kerb: Red/white inside kerb, 30 mm, full arc, plus a flat exit strip on the outside so that a kart running wide off the wider entry does not trip.
corners.runoff: Sized against 138 km/h, and mandatory: 85 deg is over the art 7.5 threshold of 80 deg, so a run-off on the axis of the direction change is required and not optional. 8 m of apron, 28 m of gravel, foam-block stopping device behind it. A kart that loses it at the 80 km/h apex reaches the barrier at 14 km/h. A kart with no brakes at all reaches it at 113 km/h, which is the case the art 7.5 numeric simulation exists for and which this first-order estimate cannot settle.
corners.rollover_note: Right-hander, 2.81 g threshold, 1.59 g sustained. Margin 1.77x, the largest on the circuit.

corners.name: T5
corners.provokes: The #32 corner - 'the inside rear visibly lifts'. It is the only sustained left in the forward lap and it is deliberately the fastest thing on the pan: 79 m of arc entered at 113 km/h and left at 128 km/h, so the lateral load BUILDS through it rather than being set at turn-in. The kart is on a 2.43 g rollover threshold turning left, against 2.81 g turning right, because 27 kg of engine sits 41 mm right of the centerline. Margin at the exit is 1.31x, the tightest on the lap, and it is held for 2.2 s - long enough for the HUD's 0.5 s sustained-g gate and long enough to judge by feel.
corners.cliff_note: Design line radius 69.3 m, on the 1.86 g plateau. Lock demand is small; what is not small is the roll moment.
corners.kerb: Red/white inside kerb, 30 mm, over the last 40 deg only. Nothing on the first 30 deg, because a kerb at the point where the inside rear is about to leave the ground is a launch ramp and #32 wants the lift to be legible, not violent.
corners.runoff: 70 deg is under the 80 deg threshold. 8 m apron, 22 m gravel on the outside of the arc, smooth barrier. Sized against the 128 km/h exit: a kart that loses it there reaches the barrier at 106 km/h if it goes straight on, but the departure angle off a 65 m radius is shallow and the barrier is the art 8 small-angle type.
corners.rollover_note: LEFT-hander, 2.43 g threshold, 1.86 g sustained at the exit. Margin 1.31x. This is the deliberate one.

corners.name: T6
corners.provokes: The corner at the toe of the return ramp, and the one whose exit is metered by a compression rather than by grip. Its exit runs 32 m of flat and then hits the sag at the ramp foot: -0.50% to +7.81% at 118 km/h, 58 m of vertical curve at the legal minimum, +0.157 g. So the kart is squashed into the road exactly as it starts to climb, and the traction it finds there sets the speed at the top of the ramp 132 m later, which sets whether the pass at T7 is available. It is the least dramatic corner on the circuit and the one that most decides the lap.
corners.cliff_note: Design line radius 38.3 m, which the sweep puts at about 1.70 g - past the 32.64 m quarter-lock row and onto the shallower part of the curve. Comfortably inside the cliff, but close enough that a driver who over-slows and then adds lock to make the apex will feel the scrub start.
corners.kerb: Red/white inside kerb, 30 mm, full arc. Exit kerb on the outside, flat, because the exit line runs out onto the ramp foot where the road is about to bend upward and a raised kerb plus a sag is how you unsettle a kart with no suspension.
corners.runoff: 75 deg, under the threshold. 6 m apron, 16 m gravel, tire barrier. Sized against 130 km/h approach; a kart losing it at the 91 km/h apex needs 43 m of gravel to stop straight-on and reaches the barrier at about 55 km/h, which the tire barrier absorbs.
corners.rollover_note: Right-hander, 2.81 g threshold, 1.70 g sustained. Margin 1.65x.

corners.name: T7
corners.provokes: The blind crest, and the whole argument of the design in one corner. It is split into two 45 deg halves of the same radius so that the grade break can sit at their junction rather than at a segment end: +7.81% to -0.70%, 8.51% of change, laid on the 211.7 m convex radius the rule allows at 56 km/h. That is 18.0 m of vertical curve, 9.0 m either side, inside two 14.14 m arcs. At any faster point on the lap the same break would need between 700 and 1300 m of radius and would not fit anywhere. So the switchback is at the top of the ramp because that is the only place on the circuit where the ground is allowed to do this. The kart goes 0.118 g light at the apex - the legal maximum unloading, -20.7 kgf on 175 kg - while turning at 0.97 g on a locked rear axle, which is #32's mechanism provoked at the slowest corner on the lap where it is safe to provoke it. And you cannot see it: sight distance through the whole uphill braking zone is under 60 m and 31 m at turn-in, 1.97 s.
corners.cliff_note: Design line radius 22.8 m, which the sweep puts at about 1.06 g - past quarter lock, in the scrubbing region, and that is intentional. This is the one corner on Cava Vecchia that makes #137 part of the racing rather than a defect you read about. It is deliberately NOT at 11 m: the test track already has the corner that walks into the cliff and stops. This one asks the driver to find the last few degrees of lock that still pay, uphill, blind, with the rear going light over the brow. If #137 is ever fixed this corner becomes a normal slow hairpin and loses nothing; if it is not, it is the corner that teaches it.
corners.kerb: Red/white inside kerb over the entry half only, 30 mm. Nothing on the exit half - the exit half contains the crest and a kerb under a kart that is 11.8% light is a kart that is airborne.
corners.runoff: MANDATORY: the two halves together are a 90 deg direction change, over the art 7.5 80 deg threshold, so a run-off on the axis is required. The axis points straight on up the hill, into the old highwall, which is the best run-off on the circuit and free from the site: 6 m of apron graded to the art 7.5 maximum 10% up-slope, then 22 m of gravel bed also rising, then a tire barrier against the rock. Sized against the 130 km/h ramp-top speed. A kart that loses it at the 56 km/h apex stops in 12 m of gravel; the up-slope is doing work the flat run-offs elsewhere cannot.
corners.rollover_note: Right-hander, 2.81 g threshold, 1.06 g sustained. No rollover risk. But in the reverse layout it is a LEFT hairpin taken over the same crest with the kart 0.118 g light, entered downhill where braking is only 1.45 g effective instead of 1.61 g. Same geometry, materially harder.

overtaking.where: T4 Il Frantoio, braking from the pan straight at 779 m
overtaking.mechanism: Entry width, not braking distance. The tow is the full pan straight plus the 97 m of T3 in front of it, all of it taken without lifting at 125 km/h or better, so a following kart arrives with real closing speed rather than with whatever it saved in the last corner. The braking zone is 33 m, which is all this kart has from 138 km/h and is not where the pass is won. The pass is won because the entry is 14 m wide - 6 m more than the regulation floor - which holds two lines side by side at 80 km/h, and because the corner is 85 deg so both lines survive to the apex.
overtaking.why_it_sticks: T4 is a right and T5 is a left, 64 m apart. The defender who takes the inside at T4 apexes early, exits slow and finds himself on the left of Il Piazzale, which is the wrong side for a 79 m left-hander that is on the throttle for its whole length. The attacker who was forced around the outside exits on the natural line and arrives at T5 with the road. It is a switchback, and it is 79 m of corner long, so it resolves rather than dangling.

overtaking.where: T7 Il Ciglione, braking uphill from La Rampa at 1237 m
overtaking.mechanism: A 194 m straight, the last 132 m of it climbing at 7.81%, into a 90 deg switchback at 56 km/h - and the whole braking zone is blind. Braking uphill is 1.61 g effective against 1.53 g flat, so the zone is 33 m rather than 35 m and the braking point is later than it looks; a driver who trusts the flat-ground reference brakes too early and hands over the inside. Sight distance measured on the built profile is 62 m at 1190 m, 44 m at 1210 m and 31 m at turn-in.
overtaking.why_it_sticks: The exit is the top of the hill and the whole 188 m start straight falls away from it at -0.70%. A defender who takes the inside gets a slower apex, and the crest inside the corner takes 11.8% of normal load off the driven axle exactly when he needs to get back on the throttle. The kart with the better exit is ahead by T1 whether or not it was ahead at the apex, and there is no corner in between to hide in.

overtaking.where: T2 Il Ciglio, braking along the bench at 310 m - secondary
overtaking.mechanism: 154 m of bench straight into the biggest speed change on the lap, 137 to 67 km/h, 37 m of braking, 11 m of entry. It is a real move and it is available on lap one, but it is the third-best of the three because the entry is only 11 m and the corner is 45 deg, so a defender can cover the inside without compromising much.
overtaking.why_it_sticks: It sticks or it does not, immediately: the exit tips over the crest of the face into 82 m of 8% descent and then a 157 m straight. Nothing on the circuit punishes a compromised exit for longer. That cuts both ways, which is what makes this the corner where a race is thrown away rather than won.

elevation.story:
The elevation is the reason the corners are where they are, and it does three jobs. It puts the slow corners at the two ends of the height change, because R = V^2/K allows a violent gradient break only where the kart is slow: T2 sits on the rim because the 5.0% break into the face needs 43 m of road at 114 km/h and 199 m at 137 km/h, and T7 sits at the top of the ramp because its 8.5% break needs 18 m at 56 km/h and 1,100 m at 137 km/h. It puts the fastest part of the lap at the bottom of the hill, where the kart arrives at 135 km/h out of an 82 m descent and is then compressed into the road at the legal maximum +0.157 g - +27.5 kgf - just before the only fast 90 deg corner on the circuit. And it makes the same 8% of gradient two different problems in one lap: you fall down it at full throttle in sixth reaching 136 km/h, and you climb the other one in third and fourth and then brake up it, blind, at 1.61 g effective instead of 1.53. Nothing else on the circuit is repeated; the gradient is, deliberately, and the reverse layout swaps which is which.

Total range is 11.42 m, and that number is not a taste call: it is what the return ramp can pay for. La Rampa plus the entry half of T7 is 146.3 m of climbing road, and at 7.81% - the steepest sustained gradient anywhere on the circuit - that buys 11.42 m and no more. Lengthening the ramp is capped by the 200 m straight rule, which the ramp plus its foot already fills to 194.34 m. So the bench sits 11.4 m above the pan because that is the height a legal kart circuit on this site can climb back. Eleven and a half metres is also exactly a working quarry bench: face heights are typically limited to 10-15 m by excavator reach and by the height at which a face can be safely scaled, so the site and the regulation happen to agree.

Drainage falls out of the same shape and has a real answer, which a flat field would not. The bench carries a 2.0% cross-fall INTO the hill - never over the crest of a face, which is how you undercut and lose it - and a -0.70% along-fall to its northern end, where a cut-off drain takes the water down the side of La Discesa. The pan straights are longitudinally flat at 0.00% and drained purely by their 2.0% cross-fall, which is what the 1.5-3.0% rule is for and is why no straight on this circuit is ever built flat in section. The whole pan then falls at -0.50% from La Sponda through T6 to the foot of La Rampa, which is the lowest point on the lap at -10.80 m and is the quarry's own sump: the settling pond that gives T5 and La Sponda their names sits behind the barrier on the outside of that corner and takes everything.

vertical_curves.note: The bench edging onto the lead-in grade. Half-length 7.7 m, and it begins 34.3 m after T2's exit, so it is clear of the release section the 2026 text asks to keep clear. Vertical acceleration 0.118 g, the convex legal maximum.

THE BLIND CREST. Half-length 21.6 m against 30.98 m of lead-in band before it and 81.98 m of face after it. Sight distance on the built parabolic profile is 58.7 m, 1.86 s at 113.8 km/h; measured numerically on the un-rounded piecewise profile it falls to 38 m, so 38-59 m is the honest bracket. Either way the road ahead disappears and the kart goes 0.118 g light as it does. Splitting the 7.30% total change into 2.30% here and 5.00% there is what makes it fit at all, and it is also what a quarry looks like: a haul road does not fall off a bench edge in one break.

THE COMPRESSION, and the fastest point on the lap. Half-length 36.7 m against 81.98 m of face before it and 41.98 m of La Conca after it - the tightest fit on the circuit, with 5.3 m to spare before T3's 4 m brush of the brakes. Built at the minimum radius on purpose, so it delivers the legal maximum +0.157 g: +15.7% normal load, +27.5 kgf on a 175 kg kart, arriving 39 m before the turn-in to a 90 deg corner.
The pan tipping into its drainage fall towards the sump. 2.7 m either side; invisible to drive and included only because it is a gradient change and the rule does not care how small.

The foot of the return ramp: the second compression, also at the legal maximum +0.157 g. Half-length 29.0 m into 62.17 m of ramp foot, so it begins 33.2 m after T6's exit and is clear of the release. Piede della Rampa is 62 m long for exactly this reason and for no other.

THE CRESTED APEX. Half-length 9.0 m inside two 14.14 m corner halves. This is the only vertical curve on the circuit that sits inside a corner, and the only reason it can is that the corner is 56 km/h: at 118 km/h the same break needs 730 m of radius and 62 m of transition, which is four times the arc available. 0.118 g of unloading at the apex of the tightest corner on the lap, on a kart with no suspension and a locked rear axle. Sight distance 30.8 m, 1.97 s.

reverse.character:
It is a different circuit because the elevation is the same and the direction is not. Every corner changes hand: T1, T2, T3, T4, T6 and T7 all become lefts and T5 becomes a right, so the forward lap's single 2.43 g-threshold corner becomes six of them and the reverse lap's hardest sustained load moves to T3-reversed - a 90 deg LEFT held at 1.85 g for 2.8 s with a 1.31x rollover margin, against 1.52x for the same corner forwards. If you want to see the inside rear lift, drive it backwards.

The two gradients swap jobs and that changes more than the view. La Rampa becomes a 132 m descent at -7.81% straight into the compression at its foot, so instead of climbing to a blind hairpin you fall towards a fast left with +15.7% of load arriving mid-braking. Il Salto becomes an 82 m climb at +8.00% that you enter at 132 km/h out of La Conca and leave at 134 km/h over a double crest onto the bench, and then brake for T2 - which means the reverse lap's hardest single moment is braking at 134 km/h over the top of a hill on the rim of an 11 m face, where the forward lap's equivalent moment was a slow corner already taken. And T7 reverses from an uphill blind hairpin approached at 1.61 g of effective braking to a downhill one approached at 1.45 g, 15% more braking distance, on a corner whose exit now falls away instead of opening out.

Measured reverse: 1340.97 m, closure 0.0157 m, final heading -360.000 deg, 43.90 s - eleven hundredths quicker than forwards, which is a coincidence of the same road at the same limits and not a design intent. All six vertical curves pass in reverse as well as forwards, but only after the geometry was changed to make them: see what_breaks.
overtaking_spots: T6 Il Sasso reversed, at 298 m. The 132 m descent of La Rampa at -7.81% arrives at 132 km/h into a compression and then a 91 km/h left-hander. Braking downhill is 1.45 g effective against 1.53 g flat, so the zone stretches to 33 m, and it sits on top of the sag - the kart is 15.7% heavier through the middle of it, which rewards a driver who trusts the load and punishes one who brakes to the flat-ground reference. Best passing place on the reverse lap and it does not exist forwards, because forwards this is a climbing acceleration zone.

T2 Il Ciglio reversed, at 1013 m. The 82 m climb of Il Salto at +8.00% into a 67 km/h left at the top, with 29 m of uphill braking at 1.54 g effective. The pass has to be complete before the crest because the exit is onto the bench and then 154 m to T1. In the forward direction this same piece of road is the fastest thing on the circuit and no passing happens on it at all.
reverse.what_breaks:
Three things, and the first is not a detail.

1. THE VERTICAL PROFILE DOES NOT REVERSE FOR FREE, and the first two versions of this layout were illegal backwards. ADR-0046 makes reverse an authored layout because curbs, run-off and sector marks do not reverse meaningfully - it does not mention elevation, and elevation is the thing that actually breaks. R = V^2/K is speed-dependent and speed is direction-dependent: the crest at the top of Il Salto is taken at 114 km/h forwards and 134 km/h backwards, so the same grade break needs 864 m of radius one way and 1,201 m the other, and the transition grows from 43 m to 60 m. In the first geometry it did not fit and the following break's transition then overlapped the reverse braking zone for T2 by 11 m. It was fixed in the BUILT ribbon, not in the layout: Il Salto's 7.30% total change was split into a 2.30% band and a 5.00% band with a 31 m lead-in between them, and the bench approach was lengthened from 30 m to 42 m. Both directions now pass. A reverse layout cannot fix this by authoring - it is geometry - so the check has to happen before the ribbon is built, which means track.json validation must run the vertical-radius test in both directions.

2. Curbs are on the wrong side everywhere, and three of them are actively dangerous rather than merely wasted. T5's kerb is on the last 40 deg of the arc because that is where the load peaks forwards; reversed, that is the turn-in and it is a launch ramp under a kart that is about to be a right-hander. T7's entry-half kerb becomes an exit-half kerb, which puts a raised kerb under a kart that is 11.8% light over the crest. T2's raised outside kerb faces the face crest in both directions, which is the one that is right by accident. The reverse layout re-specifies all seven.

3. Run-off is sized for the wrong speeds at four corners. T6 forwards is approached at 130 km/h and gets 6 m of apron and 16 m of gravel; reversed it is approached at 132 km/h off a descent with a compression in the braking zone, and 16 m is not enough - it needs the T4 treatment. T2's run-off is sized against a 137 km/h forward approach and reversed it is approached at 134 km/h, so that one survives. T7's uphill gravel bed becomes a downhill one in the sense that matters: a kart that overshoots reversed is travelling down the ramp axis, not up the hill, so the mandatory axial run-off for that 90 deg change points somewhere entirely different and has to be built twice - which is the one place this circuit costs real money to run both ways.

4. Sector marks land mid-corner if mirrored. Forward's 461 m mark mirrors to 880 m, which is inside the reversed Il Salto climb and is fine; forward's 975 m mark mirrors to 366 m, which is 24 m inside T5-reversed. The reverse layout authors its own at 362 m and 851 m.

sectors.rationale: Line to the middle of the descent. 14.67 s, 33.3% of the lap. The mark sits 21 m before the compression's vertical curve begins, on the 8% face, which is the last flat-in-plan place before the pan. Sector 1 is the whole bench, the first corner, the biggest braking zone and the drop: it is the sector that measures whether a driver committed at Il Salto.

Descent to the pond bank. 15.69 s, 35.7%. The mark is 14 m into La Sponda, on a straight, clear of T5's exit by 20 m. Sector 2 is the entire fast half - compression, Il Ventaglio, the pan straight, the overtaking corner and La Pozza - and it is the sector a slipstream shows up in.

Pond bank to the line. 13.65 s, 31.0%. The mark is deliberately BEFORE T6 rather than after it, so the whole climb - T6, the compression at the ramp foot, the ramp, the blind hairpin and the run to the line - falls in one sector. That is the sector where the lap is made, and splitting it would hide that. Reverse authors its own splits at 362 m (30.1%) and 851 m (35.1%), which are not the mirrors of these.

start_area.grid_description: Eight slots in two staggered columns on Il Banco Sud, behind the line. Row 1 at 1338.0 m, 3.0 m behind the start line; rows at a 4.0 m longitudinal pitch and a 2.6 m lateral offset, so slots occupy 1326.0-1338.0 m and 12.0 m of road. The bench is 10 m wide there and dead straight for 75 m before the line, and its gradient is -0.70%, inside the art 7.2 cap of 2% for a starting straight - which is the constraint that put the start on the bench rather than on the pan in the first place: the bench is the only made-up level terrace on the site long enough to hold a 120-200 m starting straight without a gradient. Starting lights on a gantry 12.0 m ahead of row 1, which is 9.0 m past the line, at 3.0 m above the track and spanning the centerline, per art 7.7's 10-15 m and 2.5-3.5 m. GRID SLOT SPACING IS INVENTED: REFERENCES.md records that CIK-FIA Appendices 9, 10 and 15 could not be located, so the 4.0 m pitch and 2.6 m offset are chosen to fit 8 karts on a 10 m road with a kart 1.40 m wide and about 1.80 m long, and are the single least-sourced numbers in this document.
start_area.notes: The pit lane runs outboard of the start straight, on the fill apron the quarry built along the crest of the bench for stockpiling - the widest made-up ground on the site and the reason the start complex is up here and not on the pan. Both junctions are on the RIGHT of the road, which is the side the racing line does not use at either end: a kart exiting T7, a right-hander, tracks out to the LEFT, and a kart entering T1, also a right-hander, turns in from the LEFT. So neither the deceleration lane nor the exit lane crosses the racing line, which art 7.4 requires. Deceleration lane branches at 1273.8 m, 7.9 m after T7b's exit, at 20 deg to the track, 3.5 m wide, with a chicane 14 m in per art 7.2. Exit lane rejoins at 62.0 m at 16 deg, 51 m before T1's entry. The paddock and scrutineering sit behind the pit lane on the old plant yard; the pan below carries the spectator banking, which is the one thing this site gives away free - the whole circuit except the bench is visible from the rim. A 30 km Final is 22.4 laps, so 23 laps and about 17 minutes at the estimated pace. Circuit capacity by the L/28 rule is 47.9, capped at 36; the 8-kart grid is never near it.

risks: The longest straight is 196.92 m against a hard 200 m cap - 3.08 m of margin, or 1.6%. Any later smoothing of T2's exit or T3's entry that shortens an arc lengthens that straight, and the check has to be automated rather than remembered. The same is true of the ramp run at 194.34 m.

La Conca is 41.98 m and has to hold 36.7 m of the compression's vertical curve plus 3.8 m of braking for T3. That is 1.5 m of margin on the tightest constraint in the design, and it is sensitive to T3's radius: opening T3 from 62 m to 70 m removes the braking and buys margin, but costs 30 m of lap length and makes T3 flat-out, which removes a braking reference from the fastest part of the circuit. I chose the tight version and it may be the wrong call.

The circuit is 399 x 360 m for 1,341 m of lap, which is a low-efficiency plan - a lot of the lap is spent going in straight lines across a big footprint. A real designer with the same site would fold the pan section more and get a tighter, busier circuit. The reason this one does not is that I let the two ramps and the 200 m straight cap set the shape and then closed the loop around them; a second pass would fold Il Piazzale and La Sponda into a proper esses complex and take 30 m out of the bounding box.

T7 is deliberately past #137's boundary, at a 22.8 m design line radius and about 1.06 g. If #137 is fixed by making the tire model behave past quarter lock, this corner becomes an ordinary 56 km/h hairpin and the lap loses its most distinctive corner. If #137 is fixed by REDUCING available lock, the corner may become untakeable. The design is coupled to an unresolved defect and that is a risk I am choosing knowingly, not one I missed.

Every corner speed in this document comes from a conservative line model - centerline radius plus half the road minus the kart's own 1.40 m - which is the test track's own convention. The idealised single-arc geometric line is far wider on shallow corners: T2's is 143 m against my 26.8 m, T1's is 189 m against 60.3 m. Where the truth sits between those is a racing-line question this design does not answer, and if it sits closer to the idealised end then T2 and T7 are much faster than stated and the vertical curves at those two points are all under-radiused. That is the single largest uncertainty in the whole layout and it is testable the day a lap is driven.

Lap time is a point-mass estimate with no tire scrub, no shift cuts and no line compromise, so 44.01 s is a floor. If the real number lands above 50 s the sector balance changes and the three splits will want re-authoring.

The elevation range is 11.42 m and it is bounded by the return ramp, not chosen. If a later pass wants 15 m of elevation for looks, the ramp has to get steeper than 7.81% or the 200 m straight cap has to be broken by putting a corner in the middle of the climb - and a corner in the middle of a climb is another gradient change in a curved section, which is the thing the 2026 text asks you not to do. There is no free version of that trade.

Run-off widths here are a first-order stopping-distance estimate on assumed friction - 0.45 g on compacted apron, 0.75 g on gravel - and art 7.5 explicitly requires a numeric simulation over speed, impact angle and friction coefficient. The apron and gravel figures in this document are a starting point for that simulation, not its output, and T3's in particular is not defensible as a head-on stop: a kart that goes straight on from its 125 km/h apex needs 82 m of gravel and gets 35.
outside_scope_concerns: ARITHMETIC, REFERENCES.md line ~1919 and the brief both: the 21.2 km/h concave vertical radius is given as 23 m. 21.2^2/20 = 22.47, which rounds to 22. Small, but that table is the one a designer reads to size a compression at the cliff speed, and it is the only row in it that is wrong. Every other cell checks: 143.9 -> 1380/1035, 120 -> 960/720, 100 -> 667/500, 81.3 -> 441/330, 46.0 -> 141/106, 21.2 -> 30/22.

DISAGREEMENT BETWEEN THE BRIEF AND REFERENCES.md: my brief gives the 81.3 km/h concave radius as 331 m; REFERENCES.md gives 330 m. 81.3^2/20 = 330.48, so REFERENCES.md is right and the brief drifted by 1 m. Worth knowing which document is authoritative when the two disagree.

ADR-0046'S SCHEMA CANNOT EXPRESS THE CONSTRAINT THAT NOW BINDS THE ELEVATION. The spline is specified as 'control points: position, width, banking, elevation'. A list of per-point elevations cannot say 'this grade break is laid on a 916.8 m vertical radius' - the radius becomes whatever the spline interpolation happens to produce between the samples, and the 2026 regulation makes that radius the binding elevation rule. Worse, REFERENCES.md quotes art 11 saying the longitudinal profile may be given as 'either vertical circular curves or a series of centreline levels at intervals of not less than 10 metres': the regulation offers both representations and ADR-0046 picked the one that cannot express the rule. 10 m sampling also cannot resolve this circuit's shortest vertical curve, which is 18.0 m at T7 - two samples across the whole thing. Recommend track.json carry either explicit vertical curves (station, delta grade, radius) or a validation pass that measures the induced radius from the sampled profile and asserts it against V^2/K using the speed the racing-line seed predicts there.

ADR-0046'S VALIDATION LIST IS NOW INCOMPLETE. It requires rejecting self-intersection, grid slots off the surface, unordered sector marks and 'no radius tighter than the kart can physically take'. Since #157 landed, four more items are regulation numbers with hard values and none is listed: longest straight <= 200 m (merged across collinear control points, which is the subtle part - two straight sections either side of a zero-curvature control point are ONE straight for this rule), starting straight 120-200 m, start line to first corner >= 50 m where 'corner' means a direction change >= 45 deg, and the vertical radius R = V^2/K at every gradient change. The vertical one has to run in both layout directions because V is direction-dependent; this design was illegal in reverse twice before it was legal in both.

ARCHITECTURE.md SECTION 11 STILL CONTRADICTS THE MEASURED KART. It defines a genuine overtaking spot as 'a long straight into a heavy braking zone'. This kart's longest possible braking zone is 44.0 m, from 143.9 to 60 km/h at 1.53 g - the figure is in the same repository. A design that follows section 11's wording literally will build braking zones that cannot exist. My brief already knows this and says so in Part 2; section 11 has not been updated to match, and the two documents now disagree about what an overtaking spot is.

TRACK_LAYOUT.GD'S RACING-LINE RULE IS RIGHT FOR ITS CASE AND WOULD BE BADLY WRONG IF GENERALISED. The docstring says 'with the 8 m road width the widest line through an 11 m centerline radius is about 15 m', i.e. R + W/2. For a 180 deg corner that is exactly correct - it is the arc tangent to both antiparallel outer edges. For a shallow corner it is not even close: the same construction on T2 here, 22 m radius, 45 deg, 11 m wide, gives 26.8 m by R + W/2 and 143 m by the single arc that is actually tangent to the outer edge at entry and exit and touches the inner edge at the apex, rho = (Ro*sec(A/2) - Ri)/(sec(A/2) - 1). The rule is not labelled as being 180-deg-specific and the number that follows from it - what lock the corner asks for, and therefore whether it is the safe side of #137 - is off by a factor of five if someone reuses it. It also does not subtract the kart's own 1.40 m from the usable width, which for the test track's hairpin moves 15.0 m to 14.3 m.

THE 2026 TEXT'S OWN REMEDY IS SELF-DEFEATING IN TIGHT SPACE, AND SOMEONE SHOULD KNOW BEFORE THEY TRY TO APPLY IT. Art 7.2 says R 'must be adequately increased along approach, release, braking and curved sections'. But the transition length is L = R * delta, so increasing R lengthens the curve, and a longer curve centred on the same grade break reaches FURTHER BACK into the release or braking section you were trying to keep clear. Increasing R by 30% at Il Salto's first break would have moved its tangent point from 34.3 m after T2's exit to 30.4 m after it - closer to the corner, not further. The only remedy that actually works is more distance between the corner and the break, which costs lap length. Two of this circuit's six vertical curves were sited by that arithmetic and not by the rule as written.

THE BRIEF'S CORNER-SPEED TABLE INVITES A MISTAKE IT THEN WARNS ABOUT. 'Corner speed at the 1.86 g ceiling, for reference: r=15 m 59.5, r=20 m 68.8 ...' is printed as a table with a one-line caveat that the lock sweep overrides it at small radii. The sweep says a settled 18.99 m radius is held at 0.88 g and 46.0 km/h, so the r=20 row of that table is high by 50%. Given that the whole point of Part 2 is that the sweep is counter-intuitive, the reference table is the thing most likely to be used by accident. Suggest deleting the rows below r=40 m or printing the sweep's value beside each.

MINOR, AND POSSIBLY DELIBERATE: the lock sweep is internally consistent under v^2/r for all six rows, which is worth recording somewhere because it means the 'settled radius' and 'sustained g' columns are not two independent measurements. 0.25/0.30 gives 8.60 m/s^2 against 0.88 g stated; 0.25/0.60 gives 15.62 against 1.59; 0.25/1.00 gives 18.03 against 1.84; 0.40/1.00 gives 17.83 against 1.82; 0.60/1.00 gives 9.94 against 1.02; 1.00/0.30 gives 0.90 against 0.09. All six agree to within rounding. That is reassuring for the probe but it also means a track designer using the table has one measurement per row, not two, and cannot cross-check a radius against a g independently.
